sections.h2: Who keeps property records in Miami-Dade County?
sections.html:
The Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller is the county recorder. Under Chapter 28 of the Florida Statutes, the clerk is the official recorder of every instrument that law allows to be recorded here.

The Official Records hold deeds, mortgages, liens, certain affidavits, subdivision plats, judgments, declarations of domicile, satisfactions and releases, powers of attorney and financial statements. Fees and transfer taxes are figured and collected when a document is recorded.

sections.h2: How do I search Miami-Dade Official Records?
sections.html:
Use the clerk's online Official Records search, which covers all of the instruments above. A search by name or by book and page finds the document you need.

  • Name searches work for grantors, grantees and lienholders.
  • Credit bureaus pick up liens and judgments recorded here. If a bureau reports one you do not recognize, ask them for its book and page and request a copy from the Records Library.
  • The Property Appraiser's free fraud alert, run with the clerk, tells you within 24 hours when a deed or mortgage is recorded in your name.

sections.h2: Which fees does the Miami-Dade clerk charge?
sections.html:
Most documents cost $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page. A lis pendens costs $5 for the first page and $4 for each additional page.

Source: Miami-Dade Clerk, Official Records page.

sections.h2: How do the state fee rules compare with the clerk's list?
sections.html:
Florida's clerk fee statute lists $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page of an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches, plus $1.00 for each name beyond four. It adds a $1.00 modernization charge on the first page and $0.50 on later pages, and an extra $4 per page for technology.

Plats cost $30.00 for the first page and $15.00 for each added page under the statute, and processing a tax deed application costs $60.00. The Miami-Dade clerk lists its own all-in figures, which is why the county's first-page fee reads $10.

Quote the clerk's current schedule to your title agent rather than adding statute lines yourself.

sections.h2: How much documentary stamp tax applies to a deed?
sections.html:
The clerk prints deed stamps at 60 cents per $100 of consideration, rounded up to the next hundred. Florida's revenue department confirms that Miami-Dade is the one county that uses 60 cents instead of the standard 70.

A separate surtax of 45 cents per $100 applies to transfers of real property other than a single-family residence. Mortgages pay 35 cents per $100 of the note, plus intangible tax of $2 per $1,000.

All parties to a deed are liable for the tax under state rules, regardless of who agrees to pay. Your contract with the buyer sets the practical split.

sections.h2: What goes on a mortgage, satisfaction or lien filing?
sections.html:
A mortgage must be original, signed and notarized, with a copy of the note attached or the note amount written on the face. It needs addresses for lender and borrower and a Prepared By line.

  • A satisfaction or release needs the book and page of the mortgage, the holder's signature and a notarized acknowledgement.
  • An assignment of mortgage needs the book and page, the assignor's signature and a notary.
  • A construction lien needs the lienor's signature, a notary and a legal description or property address.

A seller paying off a loan should confirm the satisfaction is recorded, then search the Official Records to see it indexed.

sections.h2: How do special deeds and court sales show up in Miami-Dade records?
sections.html:
A quit claim deed, a deed in lieu of foreclosure and a contract for deed are all on the revenue department's list of taxable documents. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable.

A foreclosure certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid. A lis pendens is the clerk's first sign that a foreclosure suit is pending, and it records at $5 for the first page.

Any buyer or seller in a distressed transfer should pull the title record before signing so every lien is in view.

sections.h2: What must a Miami-Dade deed include to be accepted?
sections.html:
The clerk's deed checklist is specific, and a missing item gets a document returned.

  • An original document with the seller's signature.
  • Addresses for grantors and grantees.
  • Two witnesses not related to the transaction, with each name and post office address printed beneath the signature.
  • A full notary acknowledgement.
  • A Prepared By statement with name and address.
  • Documentary stamps, plus the property transfer form.
  • A folio number, which is encouraged but not required, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Section 689.01 of the Florida Statutes separately requires two subscribing witnesses on a conveyance.

sections.h2: What are my options for filing a document in person, by mail or electronically?
sections.html:
There are four routes. Bring the original and fees to the Osvaldo N. Soto Miami-Dade Justice Center, mail it to the Office of County Recorder at 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, FL 33128, use an approved eRecording vendor, or use the clerk's eRecording Web Service for Notices of Commencement and Declarations of Domicile.

Electronic filings take roughly 1 to 3 business days, excluding weekends and holidays, before they appear online. The clerk says it cannot promise same-day recording, so bring time-sensitive documents in person.

Cash is accepted only in person. Credit cards are in person only, with a $5,000 daily limit.

sections.h2: Can I remove a Social Security number from a public record?
sections.html:
Yes. The clerk lets you request redaction of Social Security, bank account and credit card numbers from documents that are available online, using its online redaction form with the file number or book and page.

People covered by Chapter 119 exemptions can file a confidentiality request, in person or online. Party names stay in the index unless the name includes a street address, as in some trusts or LLCs.

sections.h2: How does the county's size affect recording and searching?
sections.html:
Miami-Dade has 975,411 households and 1,125,274 housing units, and Census data show 88.0 percent of residents had not changed address within a year. The county issued 16,535 building permits in 2025.

A county that large produces a heavy filing load, so a clean document matters. The clerk's checklist makes witness addresses and the notary block mandatory, and the clerk states it cannot guarantee same-day recording.

Search by every spelling of a name, and add the folio number when you have it, since the clerk encourages including it.

faqs.q: Where does a Miami-Dade deed get filed?
faqs.a: At the County Recorder's Office, 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, or by an approved eRecording vendor. The clerk accepts mail and in-person filings as well.

faqs.q: How much is the recording fee for a Miami-Dade deed?
faqs.a: The clerk lists $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, before documentary stamps. Statute section 28.24(13) prints a base of $5.00 and $4.00 per page and allows other charges on top, so use the clerk's list.

faqs.q: Does Miami-Dade charge a deed surtax on a house?
faqs.a: The 45 cents per $100 surtax applies to real property other than a single-family residence, so a deed for only a single-family home does not carry it.

faqs.q: Do I have to record a deed after a sale?
faqs.a: Recording is how the buyer gets public notice of the transfer. Ask the title agent to record promptly, and search Official Records afterward to confirm the deed appears.

faqs.q: How long does eRecording take in Miami-Dade?
faqs.a: Roughly 1 to 3 business days before the document is viewable online, per the clerk.
